title: Has anyone here made a multiplayer game? What was the process / outcome?
author: No_Departure7494
selftext:
Anytime I ask claude to consider making my game multiplayer it warns me "This shit gonna be fuckin' tough little man so buckle up".

I don't know many people with gaming PCs to even test it with so I kept it singleplayer.

comments.author: Masterkiefs
comments.body: Multiplayer and co op I’m such a big fan of, so it was a mandatory for me, the games built around it and it brings extra fun!

replies.author: Masterkiefs
replies.body: It’s still playable solo tho, if you do have trouble finding someone. Best of both worlds. It all depends on the game too

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body: Did you consider it from the jump? That's what it said in my prompt. That if you're gonna aim for multiplayer, start that way. Don't try to crowbar it in later.

replies.author: Masterkiefs
replies.body: Yes I did, it’s one of the early part of the builds for me. You can use steams online services or epic games, to help with the multiplayer. Then you wanna make sure the netcode is good in sync. I am sure you could ask to have it plan it for you and what that would look like, pros and cons, etc. then cross review it with another model to see if can kill the idea

comments.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
comments.body: lol, codex did it in half a day with Unity. Even made every move atomic and did checks against grifters.

replies.author: Living_Cell7304
replies.body:
Made every move atomic? Wtf does that mean?  
Are you talking about multi threading on their job system?

And unless your server is also running the simulation and only accepting inputs from the clients, it’s going to be open to cheating - no matter what “checks” you’re doing

replies.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
replies.body:
you might be right about this, frankly I’m still wrapping my head around all the way people can cheat, the AI has suggestions though, basically it amounts to this:

if it gets a command that can’t legally happen than flag it

And send a hash of the resultant state after each command so both peers can check that things are in sync

(Note: I’m making a turn based strategy so things are surely simplified in this situation)

replies.author: Living_Cell7304
replies.body:
I’ve read your other comments and you’re talking about “non-random”. The word you’re looking for is “determinism”.  
Like, deterministic random number generators, or deterministic float operations.

This leads me to believe your AI bot is either lying to you, or stretching the truth, since unity’s 2d and 3d coordinate system are highly NON deterministic, and you’d need to rip out parts of the engine to fix this.

Comparing hashes is also dumb because floating points are heavily non deterministic across different machines. Everyone is going have a different hash despite “basically the same world”.

This is sort of the problem with LLMs, it’s dumbing down the population while making people think they’re brilliant.

replies.author: theflossboss1
replies.body: Can you explain what you mean by “every move atomic”?  That is usually not the right term to describe multiplayer movement

replies.author: House13Games
replies.body: I too am somewhat sceptical about following the enthusiastic suggestions of someone who just demonstrated they have absolutely no fucking clue what they're talking about.

replies.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
replies.body: I worked professionally for triple A video game devs and indie devs for nearly a decade, I have a little bit of a clue. 🕵️

replies.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
replies.body: And actually Atomic too, so if an action has effects that happen over time like animation triggers, those effects are counted for that action alone

replies.author: Hfcsmakesmefart
replies.body: I mean non random, and I mean when you make a move on one system it will do the exact same move on every other system. Randomness is of course allowed but through a shared random seed.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Making multiplayer isn't hard if you go into the game understanding that's the plan. Specifically... it's not hard if you don't care about people hacking in the game. If you're just making a casual game for friends to play with friends, you don't need to worry so much about whether a server or player's computer is handling certain calculations, so you can focus on whichever is most efficient. But for competitive games you have to start either making things server authoritative or having all players' PCs in the game check against each other (so the majority can hold random anomalies accountable.) I opted to just assume that, for my game, people are only playing it with friends that they trust enough not to try and spoof packets (the game has plenty of systems that would be broken by players who don't want other people to have fun, anyway.)

replies.author: Hotwingz66
replies.body:
Yup.

I immediately decided a p2p mp set up.
I understood what that meant for security but in the game I'm building its not that important. Nothing competitive or with an economy.

I did use a host authoritive set up to handle some decisions because I couldnt make what I wanted work differently.

Ultimately its all about goals and trade offs.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body: If you design the game with multiplayer in mind, it shouldnt be hard.  Replication and all that.

comments.author: Toastti
comments.body:
Your biggest mistake is trying to add multiplayer later in the games development lifecycle. You absolutely have to start your game with multiplayer in mind from the very very beginning 


You really want to have some networking and programming experience on your own before you jump into making a multiplayer game. Once you start having to think about what is client owned versus server owned, how you will send updates to every online player performantly etc you will run into real issues if you don't have that experience

comments.author: SomnambulisticTaco
comments.body:
Try rebuilding an abandoned game, get the feel for how everything goes together.

Grav, for example. I always liked it but devs ruined and abandoned it.

Now I’ve got non steam local multiplayer including the steamdeck. It’s a learning process, and the next thing I do will be better.

comments.author: Chocoweb88
comments.body:
I've made an android card game with multiplayer pvp elements, and there's Ranked Match and leaderboard too. Unity has most of the tools and plugins for free. I used Photon Pun 2 to establish room connection.  It is free but can only hold i think 20 concurrent users, but it works well as i test play it between me and my test phones.

The issue is... I cant get players to test play my game lol. So I never tested the real capacity of the multiplayers aspect.

Claude also said it implemented anti cheating function, though im not sure how it works and if it works lol. Need real players/hackers to test it for me

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body:
Hey, my [game](https://destroy.spritefusion.com/) is multiplayer and got quiet good versus matches, here's how I handled it:

\- Try to decide early if your game will be multiplayer or not, this will influence non-negligible number of decisions (like a futile feature might make multilayer harder to handle)  
\- I use Cloudflare for handling the matchmaking and rooms, pretty solid and cheap.  
\- If you don't have technical grasp, try to partner with a programmer friend or learn how multiplayer works at high level. Not sure what to say here otherwise.. we're not there yet for an LLM to one-shot a multiplayer that works well out of the box.

comments.author: Templeshooter
comments.body: Its not hard, I fully vibe coded an alternative client for live mmorpg, and then I made a private server (although you can only walk and see the map), and now I made the fully original client-server project, with prediction, radius of vision, legality checks and everything you'd need for an online game. The connection was made first, in about 5 minutes. Claude likes to warn about long projects and then proceeds to do it in 1 evening. Like last time I asked to rewrite an entire open source app to run natively on Linux, and it warned me that it will take 6 months, but in 2 hours I had it fully working 😂

comments.author: robobax
comments.body: I set it as a requirement for my specifications and ensure that every step is tested against multiplayer constraints. Is it hard? No. Does it require thorough testing and a framework for your multiplayer design - 100%.

comments.author: SovereignFlip
comments.body: It really is a design you have to make very early in the design phase. The only game I've made with Claude started from the beginning as multiplayer. I didn't run into any problems setting it up. It's a 4X game and the engine is all custom. The multiplayer functionality is working great! I started on an ARPG that I intended to be a solo game to test the Bot Brain lab I'm building for NPCs. I later decided to make it multiplayer and totally ran into Claude going but but but but but....
